questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer:
I wanted to go to a country that was completely different from my own or what I was used to so far. Japan was definitely the right choice, especially Kyoto instead of Tokyo. Kyoto is more traditional and smaller, but has everything you need. I believe I would have felt too overwhelmed in Tokyo. The cultural shock was positive, especially because everyone (from the university international center to the dorm management staff) was super helpful with everything, even the smaller stuff. I would recommend staying in a dorm, since living on your own here can be quite expensive (and boring). Taishogun International House has been perfect for me: not only you're surrounded by amazing people, but all the furniture etc is in good condition. As for the University, classes have been incredibly interesting and made me able to understand the Japanese culture on a deeper level. I also attended a Japanese course which unfortunately doesn't provide you with any ECTS, but it was worth it, as now I'm already at a good conversational level, after only 4 months.
Overall, I would 100% recommend this exchange, especially to students who are attracted by what's different.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: It was way easier than I thought, both the International Center and the Dorm's staff provided me with all the necessary pieces of information and deadlines.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: They even came with me to different places (e.g. the bank, the immigration office), to help me set up all the documents I needed, since I didn't understand Japanese when I arrived. They have brochures available, and they are extremely helpful even by e-mail.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: On campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
questions.answer: There were three different international dorms, with different facilities/prices. I would recommend Taishogun I-House, as it's the best compared to the other two (quality/price-wise)

questions.question: What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
questions.answer: You have a common kitchen on every floor of the dorm, which is very spacious, modern, and has all the furniture you need. You also have a fridge in your room. However, there is also the possibility to eat on campus in 3 different cafeterias, and the price is super cheap compared to eating outside.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living in on campus housing? *
questions.answer: I would recommend it instead of finding your own apartment, as everyone will be studying with you, you will feel less lonely, and it will be super fun instead! We usually had some parties or dinners all together, we even traveled together around Japan sometimes.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: It all goes through the Manaba+R website, but here again, the international center is VERY helpful. They send you an incredibly detailed brochure with all the necessary information, and they're available anytime by email in case you need any help. You look for the courses from a list they send you, and then register the code of the course. After a week it gets approved and when classes start, you have one week to decide whether you like the course or not, and eventually deregister.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: Brochures, e-mail, website orientation.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I registered for all the classes I wanted to join, I felt like it was pretty easy to do so.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Choose the courses that fit easily in your schedule and that you feel are more interesting. I'd recommend choosing courses from the graduate school only, and not undergraduate, as they are more pertinent to what we study.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: The courses were on an adequate level for an MA in International Relations, and they were all focused on Japan or Asia in general, which I found helpful as in Europe we don't pay as much attention to it. I believe it was the perfect amount of study/classes, which I could balance well with my life outside class.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: I felt like the teaching styles and methods were really similar. They both relied on papers of the same length and difficulty, and group projects/presentations were very common as well. I didn't feel any discomfort or difficulty in studying here,

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
Globalization and Gender Issues — This course explores contemporary gender issues in relation to globalization, through case studies and multidisciplinary readings. It helps students identify and deconstruct the role of stereotypes in shaping policies, government interventions and social movements.
• Non-Traditional Security — The aim of this course is to learn about the changing paradigm of security studies in the 21st Century, in order to highlight major security challenges in the age of globalism.
• South Asian Studies — This program aims to build a locally-contextualized understanding of the regional history and present politico-economic and societal reality of South Asia.
• Liberal Arts Seminar — This course is designed to learn about western writers' preoccupations with Japanese culture and its customs.

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I would totally recommend Liberal Arts Seminar, with Chris Summerville. He has been an amazing professor, and helped us dig deeper on the Japanese culture.

questions.answer: No unexpected costs.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Transport was way more expensive than I thought, and local insurances (which are mandatory) were expensive as well.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: I joined the University's gym and pottery club, although they had around 150 different clubs that you could choose from. They were all of different kinds, from sports activities to art, to professional work, to the cinema, etc. There is one club for anything you would like to do! Even NGOs etc.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Definitely the pottery club! It's an interesting way of relaxing from all the academic stress, and you learn the Japanese way to work with clay!

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Even if it is expensive, travel around as much as you can! Kansai area is beautiful and definitely worth a visit. Take a train and go to Hiroshima, Miyajima, Okayama, Tokyo, etc. You won't probably have another chance of living in Japan for so long!

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: It was way easier than I thought, but then again, everybody was super helpful if you had any minor/major inconvenience. The language barrier was hard at first, but with the Japanese language course now I am able to communicate with anyone.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Japanese people don't speak much English, and that was really hard at first. However, after a couple of weeks you start to understand how they think and act, and you can work on it.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The food!!! Everything is delicious and affordable.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1. Don't be afraid, it will be the best 6 months of your life!
2. Travel around as much as you can while you're here, have as many experiences as you can, try different foods, go to temples, and go hiking on a random mountain. You will be able to appreciate the small things in life.
3. Learn the language while you're here, even if you don't want to work or come back here in the future. It will be helpful for you anyway.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Definitely read a guide about Japan before you come, and maybe learn some Japanese before coming here as well!

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Being able to experience a different culture, and being able to speak some Japanese only after 4 months.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: The language barrier at first, but it is an obstacle that you can easily overcome after a while.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
